current_row.boundary_rationale: A case-law analogy opens the chapter: “They say, ‘If a man puts away his wife, and she goes from him, and becomes another man’s, should he return to her again?” (web:Jer.3.1). The verse opens on a bound, dependent infinitive with no governing verb of its own, לֵאמֹ֡ר (oshb:Jer.3.1, byte tier), sitting exactly at the seam and signaling dependence on what precedes rather than supplying a formula of this unit's own; the onset warrant instead rests on the analogy's topic shift. The analogy turns to direct application at the same verse’s close: וְאַ֗תְּ זָנִית֙ רֵעִ֣ים רַבִּ֔ים וְשׁ֥וֹב אֵלַ֖י נְאֻם יְהֹוָֽה (oshb:Jer.3.1, byte tier) — “But you have played the prostitute with many lovers; yet return again to me” (web:Jer.3.1). A closure-shaped formula, נְאֻם יְהֹוָֽה (oshb:Jer.3.1, byte tier), stands at the end of this same opening verse, mid-span rather than at this unit's own close five verses later. The contiguous consonantal run of this plene spelling, shuv, stands at 41 verses book-wide at skeleton tier, the earliest of those 41 at Jer.3.1; the broader return root inflects earlier still, in its own attested spellings at וּמְשֻֽׁבוֹתַ֨יִךְ֙ (oshb:Jer.2.19), יְשִׁיבֶ֑נָּה (oshb:Jer.2.24; a single-witness ketiv/qere note also stands at that verse, נפשו נַפְשָׁהּ֙, not on the spliced word) and שָׁ֥ב אַפּ֖וֹ (oshb:Jer.2.35). The address continues through the bare-heights imagery (web:Jer.3.2) and the withheld-rain consequence (web:Jer.3.3) to a quoted plea at web:Jer.3.4-5. This unit’s onset rests on the analogy’s topic shift rather than a formula or imperative, so it is held at reduced confidence; a fresh scene, marked by a dated speech-introduction, opens the next unit at Jer.3.6 (oshb:Jer.3.6).
